abstract: Bacterial flagella are known for facilitating motility to support nutrient acquisition and predator evasion, but can also serve as receptors for phages. Here, we characterize a dual role of flagella during infection of Yersinia enterocolitica by phage X1: functioning as a conduit for phage DNA entry and as a trigger for bacterial defense. X1 employs a "contraction-driven" mechanism, using its contractile tail to inject DNA into Yersinia flagella. Unlike other characterized flagellotropic phages that rely exclusively on flagella or less efficiently on secondary surface receptors, X1 can infect cells via lipopolysaccharides with even higher efficiency. Furthermore, certain Yersinia strains can detect X1 invasion and activate a flagellum-dependent toxin-antitoxin (Flag-TA) system, which requires the flagellar motor stator proteins MotAB to activate the abortive infection response. Our findings reveal a novel phage infection strategy and uncover a new bacterial defense that are both based on the flagellar machinery.

EnglandNucleic Acids Res04110110305-10480Bacterial Proteins0DNA, Viral0LipopolysaccharidesIMYersinia enterocoliticavirologygeneticsmetabolismFlagellavirologymetabolismgeneticsBacteriophagesgeneticsphysiologyBacterial ProteinsmetabolismgeneticsDNA, ViralmetabolismgeneticsLipopolysaccharidesmetabolismBacterial flagella are best known for enabling motility, helping cells move toward nutrients and evade threats, but they can also serve as viral receptors, allowing phages to reach the bacterial surface and inject DNA. This study shows that phage X1 exploits the flagellum of Yersinia enterocolitica to inject its DNA through a contraction-driven mechanism, enabling the DNA to travel inside the filament directly into the cytosol and bypass membrane barriers. Remarkably, some Yersinia strains detect this invasion and activate a flagellum-dependent toxin–antitoxin defense system that requires the motor proteins MotAB. This abortive infection sacrifices infected cells to protect the population. These findings reveal a dual role of flagella in viral entry and bacterial immunity, uncovering a new layer of host–phage interactions and expanding our understanding of flagellum function.© The Author(s) 2025.
